extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and researchers interested in diagrammatic reasoning and Euclidean practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for the use of diagrams in Euclidean geometric demonstration (especially reductio), and for the roles of proposer, objector, and probe in traditional geometrical practice. Focuses on what diagrams may/must indicate, priorities among conditions, and practices for handling case-variants and objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductio hypothesis form and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis for reductio is, in diagrammatic form, a conjunction C1 & ... & Cn & ¬D1 & ... & ¬Dm; each ¬Dj typically reduces to a disjunction of diagram conditions producing an exponential explosion of case distinctions, so m is unlikely to be greater than one in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly represent the positive conjuncts as diagram conditions; recognize that negated diagram-conditions expand into many cases. Practical guidance: avoid building reductio steps that require tracking large disjunctions of diagram conditions; prefer formulations with small m (often m=0) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram-based reductio must lead determinately to a diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: In diagram-based reasoning, reductio gets its grip only when it leads determinately to a diagram; vague, inarticulate denials like ‘Things are not like this’ are ineffective for diagram-based reductio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not start a diagram-based reductio with an unanalyzed global denial. The hypothesis for reductio should be given in terms that can be unpacked into diagram conditions so that the diagram can be read to produce the contradiction. (Anti-pattern: attempting reductio without a determinate diagramic representation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat equivalent text-roles equivalently in the diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: It appears preferred to treat equivalently in the diagram items which play equivalent roles in the discursive text; even when the diagram cannot be subjected to all conditions in the discursive text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two elements play symmetric or equivalent roles in the verbal argument, represent them equivalently in the diagram (e.g. break both EG and FG rather than only one) to avoid asymmetrical readings that could mislead later inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority to conditions earlier in discursive text
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a choice among exact conditions to subject the diagram to, there is a priority to subject the diagram to those indicated first in the discursive text (or to those in force before the scope of a reductio), over those arising later within the reductio scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When not all textual conditions can be represented, prefer earlier-listed or pre-existing exact conditions; this supports sequential display and the flow of the proof (set out claim first, then introduce reductio hypothesis). Example: in I.6 the diagram is subjected to all exact conditions except the one arising from the reductio hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram must be suitable for sequential display of the demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams should be constructed so they can be displayed sequentially as the proof proceeds: set out the claim first before announcing and diagramming the reductio strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design initial diagrams to reflect the claim (and conditions in force entering the reductio), so later steps can be read off or introduced without reworking the diagram mid-proof. This informs choices about which conditions to represent initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram indicates all co-exact conditions from reductio hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagram indicates all co-exact conditions from the hypothesis for reductio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming the reductio diagram, represent all co-exact (contiguity/topological) aspects of the hypothesis so that the diagram captures the relevant configuration for the argument. (This is stated as a principal standard: item 2 of 4.5.5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram relationship to entering conditions is unaffected by reductio context
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship of the diagram to conditions in force upon entering the reductio context is unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions that were in force when the reductio context was entered should remain represented and respected in the diagram; do not reinterpret or drop entering conditions simply because a reductio is being attempted. (Principal standard: item 1 of 4.5.5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams may be subject to some but not all exact conditions from reductio hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagram may be subjected to some exact conditions from the hypothesis for reductio—but not all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept selective suspension of certain exact conditions in the diagram when required by reductio, but be explicit about which exact conditions are retained and which are not. Be prepared to justify why some exact conditions are not represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undercut attribution licenses that contradict earlier exact conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: One may single out co-exact conditions for which attribution licenses are undercut when such attributions, taken alone, would directly contradict exact conditions from among the Ds to which the diagram is not being subjected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If attributing a co-exact feature from the diagram would contradict an exact textual condition that is being retained, block that attribution. This selective defeasibility regulates which diagram-based attributions are legitimate in reductio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do case distinctions when diagramic support for uniform proceeding is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi-semantic artifacts (diagrams/models) provide less uniform proceeding than ordinary discursive text; the appropriate solution is case distinction. If different diagrams could affect the argument, consider them as cases and analyze them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagram production/reading is non-uniform (different d-type artifacts might satisfy constraints differently), deploy explicit case analysis rather than reading off a universal negation from a single diagram. Failure to consider relevant diagram types is a legitimate objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on reading off negations that are not diagram conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most negations of exact conditions are not diagram conditions and hence are not explicit in diagrams; reading off ¬e from a diagram is often blocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conclude ¬e purely from the appearance of a single diagram unless ¬e corresponds to an explicit diagram condition. Instead, use case analysis or other arguments to establish negations required for reductio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either redesign diagram to avoid spurious attributions or justify blocking their attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a diagram would produce spurious attributions (e.g., making a pentangle look like a triangle), either redesign the diagram (curve lines, add circle arcs) to remove the spurious feature, or provide a principled reason to disqualify or block the problematic attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two remedies: (a) redraw (e.g., use circular arcs or curved segments) so unwanted attributions vanish; (b) adopt a selective reading rule (e.g., refuse to read broken lines as separate segments) that disqualifies the objection-raising attribution. Be explicit which remedy is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for straightness when text indicates straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: There appears to be a preference for representing lines as straight when the discursive text puts forward straight lines, even if curving them could avoid problematic features; straightness offers stronger control and reduces atypical spurious regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor straight-line representation for elements verbally described as straight, unless there is a compelling reason to use curved representation. Rationale: straightness discipline gives the most powerful control and minimizes atypical diagrammatic features that provoke case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposer-of-a-case bears burden to show proposition holds in the variant
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposer of a case ‘has to show that the proposition is true of it’; a case shows how a protagonist’s claim applies to a variant diagram topologically inequivalent to those considered by the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When raising a case-variant, supply a proof or argument demonstrating the proposition holds in that variant; cases should preferably be analogous to the original proof and address the same structural issues. If the proposer fails to prove it, the burden may remain with them (pedagogical justification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection distinct role: raise an absurdity; opponent must refute
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection (enstasis) opposes either the construction or the demonstration to show an absurdity in the proof objected to; the objector need not prove anything—rather the opponent must refute the objection and show the objector is in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections function to block arguments; when an objection is raised, respond by demonstrating why the objection fails or by modifying the argument. Distinguish objections from cases: a case proves the claim in another context, while an objection shows an absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probing as central critical role
rubrics_metrics.description: Probing is the practice of critical scrutiny in geometric practice: probing case-branching control (searching for alternative diagrams satisfying textual conditions) and appearance control (resolving which metric readings of a diagram are appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain active probing of diagrams to manage open-endedness in diagrammatic reasoning. Probing may take the form of surveying metrically relaxed variants, adducing reductio arguments to exclude variants, or producing direct arguments showing a particular variant is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use verbal supplementation when diagram implicitness risks misreading
rubrics_metrics.description: When an initial diagram leaves contiguity or side relations implicit and susceptible to misinterpretation, supplement the statement verbally (e.g., add ‘not lying on the same side’) to remove ambiguity and enforce appearance control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the diagram alone could be read in multiple incompatible ways, include explicit discursive constraints in the proposition statement to avoid ambiguity. Example: Proclus/Porphyry counterexample shows 'not lying on the same side' cannot be omitted from I.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the repertoire of variant diagrams to keep case analysis manageable
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional practice relies on a modest, constrained repertoire of diagram variants such that for any elementary argument only a finite and manageable set of alternative diagrams need be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect case-branching control to be limited in practice; aim to identify the finite family of relevant variants (often located by metric distortions) rather than an open-ended search. Modern formal methods (e.g., Tarski) make this more explicit, but traditional practice operated under practical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: When appearance-control failures occur, respond by probing or subsidiary argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If an initial diagram is ambiguous due to metric sensitivity (e.g., almost-tangent circles), respond by probing the variant diagrams and, when necessary, add subsidiary proofs (direct or reductio) to resolve which variants are viable for the application at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss appearance-control challenges as merely pedagogical; provide targeted additional arguments (like III.2 supporting III.13) or redesign the diagram to ensure the main argument remains valid under the plausible variants.
